issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court exceeds its jurisdiction by disturbing concurrent findings of fact without identifying a genuine question of law.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both found that the property fell within the area covered by the notifications and that the civil court lacked jurisdiction over the landlord’s ejectment suit.

The High Court reversed those concurrent findings based on the placement of a land-record number in one notification column, without considering the notifications’ objects or explaining what legal principle of construction raised a question of law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court patently exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure; its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not permit a second appellate court to disturb concurrent findings of fact without a legally reviewable issue. The Court relied on Deity Pattabhiramaswamy v. S. Hanyamayya, AIR 1959 SC 57; Sri Sinha Ramanuja Jeer v. Shri Ranga Ramanuja Jeer, 1962 (2) SCR 509; Nedunuri Kameswaramma v. Sampati Subba Rao, 1963 (2) SCR 208; Bhusawal Borough Municipality v. Amalgamated Electricity Co. Ltd., 1964 (5) SCR 905; Secretary of State v. Rameswaram Devasthanam, AIR 1934 PC 112; Anup Mahto v. Mira Dusadh, AIR 1934 PC 5; and Sahebrao Narayanrao Deshmukh v. Jaiwantrao Yadaorao Deshmukh, AIR 1933 PC 171.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_fact_findings and high_court_reversed_those_findings and no_genuine_question_of_law_identified

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the higher court was a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual finding.
predicates.high_court_reversed_those_findings: The higher court set aside the lower courts’ concurrent factual finding.
predicates.no_genuine_question_of_law_identified: The higher court did not identify a genuine legal issue that would permit review of the factual finding.

issues.definition: When a second appeal reverses concurrent factual findings without identifying a genuine question of law, the interference exceeds jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: An area notification that identifies the relevant area as a whole is not rendered ineffective by an incomplete or inaccurately allocated land-record entry.
material_facts: A notification declared localities within a named revenue estate to be urban areas, and a later notification extended rent-control provisions to the localities covered by the earlier notification.
The house was within the named revenue estate and the specified locality.

The land-record number containing the house was listed against one locality rather than both, but the notification’s other entries indicated that the whole revenue estate and the named localities were intended to be included.
issues.conclusion: The notifications covered the property, the rent-control law applied to the tenancy, and the civil court’s jurisdiction was barred; the landlord’s suit was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 507(a) of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 concerns inclusion of areas in urban areas, and Section 1(2) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 permits extension of that Act to urban areas. The notifications must be construed as a whole, in a way that avoids absurdity; an inadvertent error in an entry does not defeat what the document’s purpose and remaining contents clearly show, applying the principle falsa demonstratio non nocet. The provisions concern areas, not individual land-record numbers.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_ejectment_dispute and notification_identifies_revenue_area_and_locality and property_within_identified_area and (land_record_entry_incomplete or land_record_number_allocated_to_one_locality)

predicates.landlord_tenant_ejectment_dispute: A landlord sought ejectment of a tenant from rented property.
predicates.notification_identifies_revenue_area_and: A notification identified the relevant revenue area and locality as areas to be included.
predicates.property_within_identified_area: The disputed property lay within the area identified by the notification.
predicates.land_record_entry_incomplete: The notification’s land-record entry did not precisely specify the location of every land parcel.
predicates.land_record_number_allocated_to_one_loca: A land-record number was entered against one locality even though the surrounding contents indicated inclusion of the wider area.

issues.definition: When an ejectment dispute concerns property within an area identified by a notification, an incomplete or misallocated land-record entry does not prevent the rent-control regime from applying.

issues.legal_issue: Inferring facts from a document generally presents a question of fact unless the interpretation requires applying a legal principle or the fact-finding court misunderstood material evidence.
material_facts: The notifications were relied on as evidence of whether the property fell within a covered area, rather than as documents establishing title.
The lower courts considered the notifications and found that the property was within the notified area.
The High Court drew a contrary inference from a land-record entry without identifying a legal principle of construction or showing that the lower courts misunderstood material evidence.
issues.conclusion: The inference from the notifications was a question of fact, not a question of law warranting interference in second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: In Nedunuri Kameswaramma v. Sampati Subba Rao, 1963 (2) SCR 208, the Court explained that construing documents produced to prove a fact does not ordinarily involve an issue of law unless material evidence was misunderstood; the documents there were not documents of title. The Court also referred to Meenakshi Mills, Madurai v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Madras, 1956 SCR 691, and held that document interpretation raises a question of law only when it involves applying a legal principle.

rule.if: second_appeal and document_used_as_evidence_of_fact and no_legal_principle_needed_for_interpretation and no_material_evidence_misunderstood

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the higher court was a second appeal.
predicates.document_used_as_evidence_of_fact: A party relied on a document to prove a factual matter rather than to establish title.
predicates.no_legal_principle_needed_for_interpreta: The document’s interpretation did not require applying a legal principle.
predicates.no_material_evidence_misunderstood: The fact-finding court did not misunderstand material evidence contained in the document.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, when a document is evidentiary and its interpretation requires neither a legal principle nor correction of misunderstood material evidence, the inference from it is a question of fact.
